title: Tokens-per-second operational buffer plan (Hosted API) - 2026Q4
body:
Purpose:
This planning note captures the operational buffer (headroom) targets for hosted API tokens/sec and QPS across regions for 2026 Q4. It is intended to be an actionable spreadsheet substitute for on-call and capacity-ops: contains assumptions, a worked example, regional buffer targets, GPU fleet mapping, and short runbook guidelines for capacity replenishment.

Context and objectives:
- Redwood’s Hosted API is encountering more bursty, long-token requests driven by multimodal assistants and long-form summarization customers. We need explicit, conservative buffers to keep 99th pct latency SLOs while minimizing overprovisioning.
- Goal: define a simple-to-operationalize buffer policy expressed as tokens/sec headroom and a QPS fallback ladder per region (NA, EU, APAC). Also map token headroom to GPU pool sizing by instance type (H100 80GB, A100 80GB, L40S) and warm capacity.

Key assumptions (model mix & cost sensitivity):
- Model mix (expected at end of Q4 workload): 60% medium-context gen (avg 256 tokens), 30% long-context gen (avg 1,024 tokens), 10% embeddings/rerank (avg 64 tokens).
- Tokenization: tokens roughly = 0.75 * characters on average; ignore small variance for planning.
- Average tokens per request (TPR): 60%*256 + 30%*1024 + 10%*64 = 358 tokens/request.
- Baseline observed 95th-percentile QPS across all regions during last month: NA 12k QPS, EU 5k QPS, APAC 3k QPS. Observed avg tokens/sec at 95th: NA 4.3M t/s, EU 1.8M t/s, APAC 1.1M t/s.
- Target SLO headroom factor: provision to sustain 1.5x 95th-percentile sustained load (this is the operational buffer). For extreme burst protection (short spikes <30s) we want burst pools that give +25% on top of the 1.5x provisioned (i.e., emergency buffer).

Worked calculations (example: NA region):
- Observed 95th tokens/sec (NA): 4.3M t/s
- Provision target (1.5x headroom): 6.45M t/s
- Emergency burst pool (25% of provision): 1.61M t/s (kept as pre-warmed pool / reserved burst nodes)
- Total operational envelope: 8.06M t/s (provision + burst)
- Translate to GPU capacity (conservative per-GPU throughput):
  * H100-80GB (optimised runtime, medium-long contexts): 250k tokens/sec per GPU (realistic for our quantized LLM mix)
  * A100-80GB: 160k tokens/sec per GPU
  * L40S (inference-optimized): 110k tokens/sec per GPU
- NA provision mapping (preferred mix H100:A100:L40S = 60:30:10):
  * Provision tokens requirement 6.45M t/s -> allocate H100 share = 3.87M /250k = ~15.5 -> 16 H100 GPUs
  * A100 share = 1.935M /160k = ~12.1 -> 13 A100 GPUs
  * L40S share = 0.645M /110k = ~5.9 -> 6 L40S GPUs
  * Total provision GPUs (NA): 35 GPUs (round up to nearest whole instance counts).
- Warm burst pool (pre-warmed): target 1.61M t/s -> prefer ephemeral A100s for faster spinup: 1.61M/160k = 10.06 -> 11 GPUs pre-warmed.
- Net NA capacity (provision + warm burst): 46 GPUs.

Regional targets (summary):
- NA (baseline 95th tokens/sec 4.3M): provision 6.45M, emergency burst 1.61M, provisioning total envelope 8.06M. CPU/GPU counts as above.
- EU (baseline 95th tokens/sec 1.8M): provision 2.7M, burst 0.675M, envelope 3.375M -> mapped to H100/A100/L40S mix -> approx 11 GPUs provision, 5 GPUs warm burst (total 16).
- APAC (baseline 95th tokens/sec 1.1M): provision 1.65M, burst 0.412M, envelope 2.062M -> approx 7 GPUs provision, 3 GPUs warm burst (total 10).

Cross-region safety and routing policy:
- Regional preference: route within region for latency; if region crosses 90% of provisioned token capacity for >60s, begin spillover to next region (NA->EU or NA->APAC depending on latency tradeoffs) but only to model variants with compatible precision/quantization.
- Priority routing ladder when region exceeds thresholds: 1) soft-throttle (reduce response length with policy header), 2) fallback to cheaper model variant in-region, 3) spill to secondary region, 4) last-resort queuing with user-facing 429/Rate-Limit hints.

Autoscaling and provisioning playbook (operationalized knobs):
- Vertical policies (fast reaction <30s): maintained by pre-warmed pool autoscheduler. Warm pool size = burst target. Pre-warmed instances are kept in idle state (model loaded, KV cache empty) and can start serving in ~20–45s.
- Horizontal ramp (minutes scale): scheduled autoscaling based on token/sec moving average (30s, 3m, 15m windows). Thresholds: 85% provisioned capacity triggered scale-up (add N GPUs), scale-down at sustained <50% for 20m.
- Cold provisioning lead time: acquiring new spare GPUs from cloud takes ~8–15 minutes to attach plus model init; therefore we keep warm pools to cover short spikes.

SLO & cost tradeoffs (policy recommendation):
- Default headroom factor = 1.5x 95th sustain. Rationale: balances cost vs. risk of hitting 99th latency degradation.
- Emergency burst (pre-warmed) = 25% of provision. Rationale: covers 90th-99th short spikes without global routing.
- If customers require lower latency at higher percentiles, propose dedicated capacity (Redwood Dedicated) rather than increasing global headroom.

Monitoring signals (must be instrumented):
- tokens/sec per-region (1s granularity), per-model family tokens/sec, 95/99/999 percentiles of queue latency, token-dropping rate, pre-warm pool utilization, model load times, GPU-side saturation signals (smem utilization, compute utilization).
- Alerts: token/sec > 90% provisioned for 60s -> P1 alert to infra on-call; token/sec > 98% for 30s -> invoke spillover runbook; sustained > 110% for 5m -> emergency exec paging and activate mass-queue mitigation.

Operational appendix (short runbook snippets):
- If NA region crosses 90% provisioned: 1) add 2 warm A100 nodes from warm pool, 2) enable soft-throttle header at edge (reduce default max_tokens by 20%), 3) notify product and CS with current ETA for spillover if >90s.
- If warm pool exhausted and 95% persists >120s: 1) trigger cross-region spill to EU (if latency delta <60ms for top customers), 2) temporarily flip non-SLA traffic to lower-cost model variant.
- Post-incident: capture token distribution, top 10 customers by token consumption, model types responsible, and evaluate whether long-term provision factor needs increase.

Open questions / action items:
- Revisit per-GPU tokens/sec numbers after H100 runtime microkernel update (PR #312) — blocker: need new benchmark matrix (Rafael).
- Decide on a permanent warm-pool instance type per region (cost vs. start-time tradeoffs). Suggest A100 in EU/APAC, H100 in NA for top-tier customers (Maya to cost model).
- Add a dashboard tile showing provisioned vs. effective headroom ratio per region (engineering metrics board).

Quick summary table (human readable):
- Headroom policy: provision = 1.5x 95th tokens/sec; emergency warm burst = +25% of provision; total envelope = provision + burst.
- NA example: 95th 4.3M -> provision 6.45M -> burst 1.61M -> envelope 8.06M -> ~46 GPUs total (provision + warm).
- EU example: 95th 1.8M -> provision 2.7M -> burst 0.675M -> envelope 3.375M -> ~16 GPUs total.
- APAC example: 95th 1.1M -> provision 1.65M -> burst 0.412M -> envelope 2.062M -> ~10 GPUs total.

Notes: this doc is intentionally conservative for Q4 with the expectation of reassessing after the next infra microkernel updates and the H100 runtime benchmarks. Use as the canonical interim plan for pre-warm sizing and the regional routing guardrails.
